/**
 * TanStack Form composition for the Pulse field controls.
 *
 * `Form` is a `<form>` that validates React Aria's own fields. This module is the other half: the
 * same controls driven by [TanStack Form](https://tanstack.com/form), where the form library owns
 * the values and this library owns how a field looks, what it says when it is wrong, and how it is
 * operated.
 *
 * ## Why `createFormHook`, and not a wrapper around each control
 *
 * The obvious shape for an integration is one wrapper component per control — a `FieldTextField`
 * taking a `name` and reaching for the form through a hook. It is the shape written by hand in every
 * app that uses both libraries, and it is wrong in a way that only shows up later: the wrapper has
 * to be handed the form, so it only works inside the component that owns it. A field inside a
 * reusable sub-form, a field group, or a `withForm` block cannot reach a form it was never given.
 *
 * TanStack's own answer is `createFormHook`, and it is the answer for the same reason React Aria
 * components here take `isDisabled` rather than `disabled`: the context is the wiring. A field
 * component reads its field from `fieldContext`, which `<form.AppField name="…">` provides, so the
 * same component works anywhere in the tree — including inside a sub-form rendered by `withForm`,
 * which receives a *different* form instance.
 *
 * The registration at the bottom is therefore the whole integration. `useAppForm` is `useForm` with
 * the field components already attached, and the render prop TanStack hands to `AppField`'s children
 * is a `FieldApi` with those components assigned onto it — which is why a consumer writes
 * `<field.TextField>` and gets this library's `TextField` bound to that field.
 *
 * ## Two things every root below does, and why
 *
 * **`validationBehavior="aria"` on every field.** TanStack owns validation here, so React Aria must
 * not also run the browser's. Left at the library default of `native`, a required field renders the
 * `required` attribute and the browser blocks submission with its own bubble — the styled message
 * never gets a chance and the two validators argue. `aria` keeps `data-required`, so the label still
 * draws its asterisk, and hands validation to the form library. `Form.tsx` records the same decision
 * made the other way round, for the forms React Aria validates itself.
 *
 * **`isInvalid` comes from the field's own errors, with no "touched" gate.** TanStack's
 * `handleSubmit` marks every field touched before it validates, so a submit-time error always shows;
 * and a validator that runs `onChange` shows as the user types, which is what that validator asked
 * for. Gating on `isTouched` as well would only ever hide errors the validator deliberately made.
 *
 * ## The one field React Aria does not supply
 *
 * `field.Slider` binds its value and its invalid state, and `field.Slider.Error` renders the
 * field's messages — but the invalid state itself is this library's, not React Aria's. `Slider` is
 * not a field there: `useSlider` takes no `isInvalid`, so `Slider` publishes the validation
 * context a `FieldError` renders from itself, and the message is the caller's rather than a
 * server's. Every other bound field here reads an invalid state React Aria computed. See
 * `docs/components/form.md`.
 */
import { createFormHook, createFormHookContexts } from '@tanstack/react-form'
import type { AnyFieldApi } from '@tanstack/react-form'
import { useContext } from 'react'
import type { ComponentType, ReactNode } from 'react'
import type { Color, DateValue, Key, TimeValue } from 'react-aria-components'

import { Button } from '../Button/Button'
import type { ButtonProps } from '../Button/Button'
import { Checkbox } from '../Checkbox/Checkbox'
import type { CheckboxGroupProps, CheckboxProps } from '../Checkbox/Checkbox'
import { ColorField } from '../ColorField/ColorField'
import type { ColorFieldProps } from '../ColorField/ColorField'
import { DateField } from '../DateField/DateField'
import type { DateFieldProps } from '../DateField/DateField'
import { NumberField } from '../NumberField/NumberField'
import type { NumberFieldProps } from '../NumberField/NumberField'
import { Radio } from '../Radio/Radio'
import type { RadioGroupProps } from '../Radio/Radio'
import { SearchField } from '../SearchField/SearchField'
import type { SearchFieldProps } from '../SearchField/SearchField'
import { Select } from '../Select/Select'
import type { SelectProps } from '../Select/Select'
import { Slider } from '../Slider/Slider'
import type { SliderProps } from '../Slider/Slider'
import { Switch } from '../Switch/Switch'
import type { SwitchProps } from '../Switch/Switch'
import { TextArea } from '../TextArea/TextArea'
import type { TextAreaProps } from '../TextArea/TextArea'
import { TextField } from '../TextField/TextField'
import type { TextFieldProps } from '../TextField/TextField'
import { TimeField } from '../TimeField/TimeField'
import type { TimeFieldProps } from '../TimeField/TimeField'
import { Form, FormActions, FormLegend, FormSection } from './Form'
import type { FormProps } from './Form'

/**
 * The two contexts `createFormHook` needs, plus the accessors for them.
 *
 * They are created once here rather than in the consumer's app, for the same reason the field
 * components live here: `createFormHook` pairs a context with the components that read it, so a
 * second `createFormHookContexts()` elsewhere would make a second, disconnected pair and a
 * `field.TextField` that throws. `useFieldContext` is exported so an app can write its own field
 * component against this library's controls and register it with `extendForm`.
 */
export const { fieldContext, formContext, useFieldContext, useFormContext } =
  createFormHookContexts()

/**
 * Every message a field is currently carrying, as plain strings.
 *
 * TanStack types `meta.errors` as "whatever the validators returned", and that is not one thing: a
 * validator function returns a string, while a Standard Schema validator — the Zod, Valibot or
 * ArkType path — returns an *issue object* with a `message` on it. Joining the array directly, which
 * is what TanStack's own examples do, renders `[object Object]` for the second kind. Both shapes are
 * read here, and anything else is dropped rather than printed.
 */
export function fieldErrorMessages(field: AnyFieldApi): string[] {
  const errors = (field.state.meta.errors as unknown[]).flat(1)
  return errors
    .map((error) => {
      if (typeof error === 'string') return error
      if (error && typeof error === 'object' && 'message' in error) {
        const message: unknown = (error as { message?: unknown }).message
        return typeof message === 'string' ? message : undefined
      }
      return undefined
    })
    .filter((message): message is string => Boolean(message))
}

/**
 * What `fieldErrorSlot` renders — the shared shape of every control's `Error` slot.
 *
 * Narrower than React Aria's own `FieldErrorProps`, and deliberately: the error slots in this
 * library publish `className?: string`, not the render function the library allows, and a factory
 * typed against the wider prop cannot be handed one of them. `string` still satisfies the wider
 * prop, so the narrower type is the one both ends agree on.
 */
type FieldErrorSlotProps = { className?: string; children?: ReactNode }

/**
 * **Every bound field's value is `T | undefined`, not `T`.**
 *
 * `useFieldContext<T>()` is a *claim* this library makes about the form it is dropped into, not a
 * constraint it can enforce: the consumer's `defaultValues` decides the real type, and a key that is
 * absent, cleared with `setFieldValue(name, undefined)`, or reached through an optional parent is
 * `undefined` at runtime whatever the cast says. Passing that straight through would flip a React
 * Aria control from controlled to uncontrolled — the one state in which the form stops owning the
 * value, which is the whole premise of this file — so every root narrows it with a default, and every
 * root declares the value as `Bound<…>` so that the default is a real branch rather than dead code.
 */
type Bound<T> = T | undefined

/**
 * Turns a control's own `Error` slot into the one a field component carries.
 *
 * With no children it renders the field's own messages, so `<field.TextField.Error />` is the whole
 * message rather than a placeholder waiting for the consumer to re-implement error extraction. With
 * children it is the plain slot again — which is what a server's answer needs, where the text is
 * known and the field's validators are not what produced it.
 *
 * It reads the context with `useContext` rather than `useFieldContext` on purpose: the throwing
 * accessor is right for a root, where a missing provider is a bug, and wrong for a slot, where it
 * would turn a misplaced slot into a crash instead of a field that renders its plain content.
 */
function fieldErrorSlot(Plain: ComponentType<FieldErrorSlotProps>) {
  function FieldError({ children, ...props }: FieldErrorSlotProps) {
    // `createFormHookContexts` builds this context with `null`, so a slot outside a field reads
    // `null` — but the type it publishes says `AnyFieldApi`, with no `| null` on it. The cast restores
    // what is actually there; without it the branch below reads as dead code, and the misplacement
    // this guards against turns into a crash instead of a field that renders its plain content.
    const field = useContext(fieldContext) as AnyFieldApi | null
    const messages = field ? fieldErrorMessages(field) : []
    return (
      <Plain {...props}>
        {children ?? (messages.length > 0 ? messages.join(', ') : null)}
      </Plain>
    )
  }
  return FieldError
}

/**
 * The props every field component publishes: the control's own, minus the ones the *field* owns.
 *
 * `value`, `defaultValue` and `onChange` are omitted rather than merely unused — TanStack's form is
 * the single source of truth, so accepting them here would silently do nothing. That is the same
 * rule `TextField` states for its own `Input`. `name` and `validationBehavior` go with them: the
 * field names the control after itself in the form's data, and it validates in `aria` mode for the
 * reason recorded at the top of this file.
 */
export type FieldTextFieldProps = Omit<
  TextFieldProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldTextAreaProps = Omit<
  TextAreaProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldSearchFieldProps = Omit<
  SearchFieldProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldNumberFieldProps = Omit<
  NumberFieldProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldSelectProps = Omit<
  SelectProps,
  | 'selectedKey'
  | 'defaultSelectedKey'
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldCheckboxProps = Omit<
  CheckboxProps,
  | 'isSelected'
  | 'defaultSelected'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldCheckboxGroupProps = Omit<
  CheckboxGroupProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldSwitchProps = Omit<
  SwitchProps,
  | 'isSelected'
  | 'defaultSelected'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldRadioProps = Omit<
  RadioGroupProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldSliderProps = Omit<
  SliderProps,
  'value' | 'defaultValue' | 'onChange' | 'isInvalid'
>
export type FieldDateFieldProps = Omit<
  DateFieldProps<DateValue>,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldTimeFieldProps = Omit<
  TimeFieldProps<TimeValue>,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldColorFieldProps = Omit<
  ColorFieldProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>

/**
 * A labelled text control bound to one string field. Use it as `field.TextField` inside
 * `<form.AppField name="…">`.
 *
 * ```tsx
 * <field.TextField isRequired>
 *   <field.TextField.Label>First name</field.TextField.Label>
 *   <field.TextField.Input placeholder="Ada" />
 *   <field.TextField.Hint>As it should appear on the invoice</field.TextField.Hint>
 *   <field.TextField.Error />
 * </field.TextField>
 * ```
 *
 * The value is a string. `Label`, `Group`, `Input`, `Icon` and `Hint` are `TextField`'s own slots
 * unchanged; `Error` is the field-aware one, and renders the field's messages when given none.
 */
function FieldTextFieldRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldTextFieldProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<string>>()
  return (
    <TextField
      name={field.name}
      value={field.state.value ?? ''}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </TextField>
  )
}

export const FieldTextField = Object.assign(FieldTextFieldRoot, {
  Label: TextField.Label,
  Group: TextField.Group,
  Input: TextField.Input,
  Icon: TextField.Icon,
  Hint: TextField.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(TextField.Error),
})

/** Several lines of text bound to one string field — `TextField`'s anatomy with a control that grows. */
function FieldTextAreaRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldTextAreaProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<string>>()
  return (
    <TextArea
      name={field.name}
      value={field.state.value ?? ''}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </TextArea>
  )
}

export const FieldTextArea = Object.assign(FieldTextAreaRoot, {
  Label: TextArea.Label,
  Input: TextArea.Input,
  Hint: TextArea.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(TextArea.Error),
})

/**
 * A search control bound to one string field.
 *
 * `onSubmit` and `onClear` still pass through, so both halves of a search field's contract survive:
 * the value on every keystroke, and the value at the moment the user says they have finished typing.
 */
function FieldSearchFieldRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldSearchFieldProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<string>>()
  return (
    <SearchField
      name={field.name}
      value={field.state.value ?? ''}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </SearchField>
  )
}

export const FieldSearchField = Object.assign(FieldSearchFieldRoot, {
  Label: SearchField.Label,
  Group: SearchField.Group,
  Input: SearchField.Input,
  Icon: SearchField.Icon,
  Hint: SearchField.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(SearchField.Error),
})

/**
 * A number bound to one field, as a `number | null`.
 *
 * `null` for empty is React Aria's own answer and the honest one: a field nobody has typed in holds
 * no number, and `0` is a number somebody could have meant. It is handed to the control as `NaN`,
 * though, because `NaN` is how *React Aria* spells empty internally — it is the value its own state
 * is keyed on, its input renders blank for it, and its stepper counts from the minimum rather than
 * from zero. `null` is what `onChange` hands back for the same state, so the two meet here and
 * nowhere else.
 */
function FieldNumberFieldRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldNumberFieldProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<number | null>>()
  return (
    <NumberField
      name={field.name}
      value={field.state.value ?? NaN}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </NumberField>
  )
}

export const FieldNumberField = Object.assign(FieldNumberFieldRoot, {
  Label: NumberField.Label,
  Group: NumberField.Group,
  Input: NumberField.Input,
  Counter: NumberField.Counter,
  Hint: NumberField.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(NumberField.Error),
})

/**
 * One choice from a list, bound to one key field.
 *
 * Single selection only. React Aria splits a select's value in two — `selectedKey` for one choice, an
 * array-valued `value` for several — and a bound component would have to switch between them on a
 * runtime `selectionMode`, which is not a shape the props can carry. A multiple select needs
 * `useFieldContext` and a component of its own.
 *
 * Every slot of `Select` is carried over, so the whole menu — `OptionList`, `Option`, `Section`,
 * `AutoComplete` — is written exactly as it is outside a form.
 */
function FieldSelectRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldSelectProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<Key | null>>()
  return (
    <Select
      name={field.name}
      selectedKey={field.state.value ?? null}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </Select>
  )
}

export const FieldSelect = Object.assign(FieldSelectRoot, {
  Label: Select.Label,
  Value: Select.Value,
  Button: Select.Button,
  Icon: Select.Icon,
  Popover: Select.Popover,
  AutoComplete: Select.AutoComplete,
  OptionList: Select.OptionList,
  Menu: Select.Menu,
  Option: Select.Option,
  Section: Select.Section,
  SectionTitle: Select.SectionTitle,
  Hint: Select.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(Select.Error),
})

/**
 * One checkbox bound to one boolean field, for a single yes-or-no — a consent, a term.
 *
 * `Checkbox.value` is deliberately left alone: inside a group that prop identifies the checkbox to
 * the group, and it is not the field's value here, so a field component has no business setting it.
 * For a field that *is* a set of checkboxes, use `field.CheckboxGroup`.
 */
function FieldCheckboxRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldCheckboxProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<boolean>>()
  return (
    <Checkbox
      name={field.name}
      isSelected={field.state.value ?? false}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </Checkbox>
  )
}

export const FieldCheckbox = Object.assign(FieldCheckboxRoot, {
  Indicator: Checkbox.Indicator,
  Text: Checkbox.Text,
  Hint: Checkbox.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(Checkbox.Error),
})

/**
 * A set of checkboxes bound to one array-of-keys field — "which of these apply".
 *
 * The individual checkboxes are plain `Checkbox`es with `Checkbox.Indicator` and `Checkbox.Text`,
 * exactly as outside a form: the group owns the array, so only the group is a field.
 */
function FieldCheckboxGroupRoot({
  children,
  ...props
}: FieldCheckboxGroupProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<string[]>>()

export type FieldFormProps = Omit<
  FormProps,
  'onSubmit' | 'validationBehavior' | 'validationErrors'
>

/**
 * The `<form>`, wired to this TanStack form. Use it as `form.Form`, inside `form.AppForm`.
 *
 * It exists to remove the two lines every TanStack form has to write correctly and can quietly get
 * wrong: `onSubmit` must stop the browser's own submission before handing the values to
 * `handleSubmit`, and `validationBehavior` must be `aria` so the browser does not validate the
 * fields a second time. Both are here, once.
 *
 * `Form`'s own layout slots are attached too, so the whole form reads in one namespace:
 * `form.Form.Legend`, `form.Form.Section`, `form.Form.Actions`.
 */
function FieldFormRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldFormProps) {
  const form = useFormContext()
  return (
    <Form
      validationBehavior="aria"
      onSubmit={(event) => {
        event.preventDefault()
        void form.handleSubmit()
      }}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </Form>
  )
}

export const FieldForm = Object.assign(FieldFormRoot, {
  Legend: FormLegend,
  Section: FormSection,
  Actions: FormActions,
})

/** The submit button's own props, minus what it reads from the form. */
export type FieldSubmitProps = Omit<ButtonProps, 'type' | 'isPending'>

/**
 * The button that submits the form. Use it as `form.Submit`.
 *
 * It is a `Button` with `type="submit"` and `isPending` already bound to the form's
 * `isSubmitting`, so the spinner, the blocked presses and the live region all come from the button
 * this system already has.
 *
 * It is deliberately **not** disabled while the form is invalid. A button greyed out with no
 * explanation is the thing validation exists to avoid, and there is no form-level message element
 * for it to explain itself in — the errors belong to the fields.
 */
export function FieldSubmit({ children, ...props }: FieldSubmitProps) {
  const form = useFormContext()
  return (
    <form.Subscribe selector={(state) => state.isSubmitting}>
      {(isSubmitting) => (
        <Button type="submit" isPending={isSubmitting} {...props}>
          {children}
        </Button>
      )}
    </form.Subscribe>
  )
}

/**
 * `useForm` with this library's fields already attached.
 *
 * Every field component above is registered by name, and the name is what a consumer writes: the
 * `field` TanStack hands to `<form.AppField>`'s children is the field API with these objects
 * assigned onto it, so `field.TextField` is `FieldTextField`. Two form-level components are
 * registered the same way — `form.Form` and `form.Submit`.
 *
 * `withForm`, `withFieldGroup`, `useTypedAppFormContext` and `extendForm` come along with it, and
 * they are why this is a hook factory rather than a component: a reusable sub-form receives its own
 * form instance, and the field components keep working inside it because they read the field from
 * context rather than from a captured form.
 */
export const {
  useAppForm,
  withForm,
  withFieldGroup,
  useTypedAppFormContext,
  extendForm,
} = createFormHook({
  fieldComponents: {
    TextField: FieldTextField,
    TextArea: FieldTextArea,
    SearchField: FieldSearchField,
    NumberField: FieldNumberField,
    Select: FieldSelect,
    Checkbox: FieldCheckbox,
    CheckboxGroup: FieldCheckboxGroup,
    Switch: FieldSwitch,
    Radio: FieldRadio,
    Slider: FieldSlider,
    DateField: FieldDateField,
    TimeField: FieldTimeField,
    ColorField: FieldColorField,
  },
  formComponents: {
    Form: FieldForm,
    Submit: FieldSubmit,
  },
  fieldContext,
  formContext,
})

import { Link as AriaLink } from 'react-aria-components'
import type { LinkProps as AriaLinkProps } from 'react-aria-components'

import {
  LINK,
  LINK_CAPS,
  LINK_CAPS_BASE,
  LINK_URL,
  LINK_VIEWMORE,
} from '../link'

/** Which of the sheet's three links this is. */
export type LinkVariant = 'caps' | 'url' | 'viewmore'

/** `.ds-link-caps--lg` only changes the type size, so it is a size rather than a second variant. */
export type LinkSize = 'sm' | 'lg'

export interface LinkProps extends Omit<
  AriaLinkProps,
  'className' | 'href' | 'isDisabled' | 'onPress' | 'target'
> {
  /** Where the link goes. It renders a real anchor, so middle-click and "open in a new tab" work. */
  href?: AriaLinkProps['href']
  /** Renders it unavailable without removing it from the page. */
  isDisabled?: AriaLinkProps['isDisabled']
  /** Press handler. This is a React Aria prop — there is no `onClick`. */
  onPress?: AriaLinkProps['onPress']
  /** The anchor's target, e.g. `_blank`. */
  target?: AriaLinkProps['target']

  /**
   * `caps` is `.ds-link-caps` — the sheet's nav and legend link. `url` is `.ds-link-url`, for a
   * destination inside running text. `viewmore` is `.ds-link-viewmore`, the accent call to go and
   * read the rest.
   */
  variant?: LinkVariant
  /** Only `caps` has two sizes, because only `.ds-link-caps` does. */
  size?: LinkSize
  className?: string
  children?: React.ReactNode
}

/**
 * The sheet's three links: `.ds-link-caps`, `.ds-link-url` and `.ds-link-viewmore`.
 *
 * ```tsx
 * <Link href="/monitors" isCurrent>Monitors</Link>
 * <Link variant="url" href="https://status.example.com">status.example.com</Link>
 * <Link variant="viewmore" href="/monitors">View more</Link>
 * ```
 *
 * React Aria's `Link` is what makes these links at all: it renders a real `<a>`, so middle-click,
 * the status bar and "open in a new tab" work, and `isCurrent` gives the page you are on both
 * `aria-current` for a screen reader and `data-current` for the sheet's own
 * `[aria-current="page"] { color: teal }` rule.
 *
 * **The three variants are three different jobs, which is why they are not one link with a colour
 * option.** Every one of them derives its hover from what it is: a caps link darkens toward full
 * strength because at 70% it is deliberately quiet at rest; a URL link turns teal because its
 * underline already carries the affordance; and a view-more link *gains* an underline, because it
 * wears the accent at rest and needs somewhere to go on hover. Swapping any two of those would say
 * the wrong thing about the link.
 */
export function Link({
  variant = 'caps',
  size = 'sm',
  className,
  children,
  ...props
}: LinkProps) {
  const variantClass =
    variant === 'url'
      ? LINK_URL
      : variant === 'viewmore'
        ? LINK_VIEWMORE
        : [LINK_CAPS[size], LINK_CAPS_BASE].join(' ')

  return (
    <AriaLink
      data-slot="link"
      className={[LINK, variantClass, className].filter(Boolean).join(' ')}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </AriaLink>
  )
}

  Link as AriaLink,

  NavigationTreeItem as AriaNavigationTreeItem,
  NavigationTreeItemContent as AriaNavigationTreeItemContent,

  NavigationTreeHeaderProps as AriaNavigationTreeHeaderProps,
  NavigationTreeItemContentProps as AriaNavigationTreeItemContentProps,
  NavigationTreeItemProps as AriaNavigationTreeItemProps,

/**
 * The sheet has **no sidebar** — its two navs, `dash-nav` and `page-nav`, are both horizontal top
 * bars — so the *arrangement* here is an invention. The *behaviour* is not: React Aria's
 * `NavigationTree` is a nested, hierarchical set of links, which is what a sidebar actually is.
 *
 * Everything visible is still the sheet's own vocabulary, turned on its side:
 *
 * - `.ds-link-caps` — 14px, `-0.01em`, uppercase, white at 70% going to white on hover — is the
 *   sheet's nav link, and it is the whole of what an item is here.
 * - The sheet's own `[aria-current="page"] { color: var(--c-teal) }` is how it marks the current
 *   page. `NavigationTree`'s `selectedRoute` produces the same thing as `data-current`, and adds
 *   `data-current-ancestor` for the parents of the current route — which a top bar never needed
 *   and a tree cannot do without.
 * - `.ds-panel` is the surface, `.ds-div-hair` divides the groups, `.ds-count` — 11px in the
 *   selected-yellow — is the badge.
 *
 * ### The four parts of a row, and why the order is the order
 *
 * A row is **an icon column, then the link, then the disclosure**. The icon leads because a sidebar
 * that carries glyphs has one column of them and it is the leftmost thing the eye lands on; the
 * disclosure trails because that is the far end of the row, where a count also lands, and because
 * the leading column is already spoken for by the icon. The reservation that used to hold a
 * chevron's box is now the **icon's** box (`NAV_ICON`), drawn on every row whether or not it has a
 * glyph, for the reason the chevron's was: a column of labels that steps in and out as the eye reads
 * down it says nothing true about anything.
 *
 * ### The rail, and what a row becomes when there is no room for a label
 *
 * `isCollapsed` narrows the panel to an icon column. A label does not fit, and dropping it would
 * take the item's *name* away with it — so it stays in the markup at zero width (`NAV_TEXT`) and
 * keeps saying "Dashboard" to a screen reader while showing nothing. Three things follow from that,
 * and each of them is why the rail is more than `w-16`:
 *
 * - **The count becomes the dot on the icon's shoulder.** A number cannot be read at 6px, but its
 *   presence can, and the number itself is still in the markup the dot clips.
 * - **The tooltip is the label.** The rail is the one place where the tooltip is the only way to know
 *   what a control is, which is what `delay={0}` is for. It hangs on a **React Aria `Link`**, not on
 *   the plain anchor the wide panel draws: `TooltipTrigger` hands its trigger its props through the
 *   Focusable context rather than by cloning, so a bare `<a>` never receives them and the tooltip
 *   would simply never open.
 * - **The disclosure goes quiet rather than away.** React Aria refuses an expandable item with no
 *   expand button, and it is right to: a rail whose branches cannot be opened is a rail that lies.
 *   So the button keeps its place in the focus order and appears in the row's corner when the row is
 *   pointed at or focused — the one thing on this surface that is invisible until you need it.
 */
/** As tall as the page it sits beside, not as tall as its links: a sidebar that stops short reads as
 * a floating panel, which is the one thing it is not. */
const NAV_PANEL = [
  'flex flex-col min-h-full',
  'border-e border-border-soft bg-card',
].join(' ')

/** The wide panel, and the rail. One or the other — never both, since two width utilities are a coin toss. */
const NAV_WIDTH = 'w-56'
const NAV_RAIL_WIDTH = 'w-16'

/**
 * Indentation by nesting depth, from the tree's own `level`. Written as whole literals rather than
 * as arithmetic on `level`, because Tailwind reads source text and cannot see a computed class —
 * the map is the only reason these three utilities exist in the stylesheet at all.
 */

  1: 'ps-[18px]',
  2: 'ps-[30px]',
  3: 'ps-[42px]',
}

 * The hairline that follows a branch down the page, drawn by every row below the first level at
 * **its parent's icon column** — 26px, the centre of a level-1 icon box that runs 18px to 34px.
 *
 * Without it, indentation is the only thing saying a row is inside another one, and an indent is a
 * measurement the eye has to take against the panel edge rather than a line it can follow. It is

const NAV_CHEVRON_RAIL = [
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:absolute [[data-collapsed]_&]:end-1 [[data-collapsed]_&]:bottom-1',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:opacity-0',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:[[data-hovered]_&]:opacity-100',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:focus-visible:opacity-100',

 * The box the row leads with, drawn even when there is no icon in it.

 * a column of edges, and a label that steps in and out as the eye reads down it is the first thing
 * anyone sees. Reserving the box on every row gives one left edge per level and one icon column down

  'grid size-4 shrink-0 place-items-center',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:size-10',

 * What the item says, wrapped so that the rail can fold it away without losing it.
 *

 * it — the dot is absolutely positioned against the row, and an ancestor's `overflow` does not reach

  'contents',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:block [[data-collapsed]_&]:w-0 [[data-collapsed]_&]:overflow-hidden',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:whitespace-nowrap',
].join(' ')

 * The anchor inside the row's content. The row is pressable and focusable and the anchor is neither
 * a second tab stop nor a second ring — it is there so the item is a *link*: middle-click, open in a

  'flex min-w-0 flex-1 items-center gap-2 text-inherit no-underline',
  // The rail: the anchor *is* the icon's box, so the link is as big as the thing it stands for and
  // the icon has no gap to centre around.
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:justify-center [[data-collapsed]_&]:gap-0',

export const NAV_HEADER = [

  // to the row above as one row sits to the next, which read as one more item rather than a group's name.
  'px-[18px] pt-5 pb-1.5',
  'text-[12px] uppercase tracking-[0.04em] text-foreground/55',

  // three wrapped words; the line the name was standing for is what is left of it, and the text stays
  // in the markup for the same reason a label does — a group a screen reader cannot hear is not
  // grouped at all.
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:mx-2.5 [[data-collapsed]_&]:my-2 [[data-collapsed]_&]:h-px [[data-collapsed]_&]:p-0',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:bg-border-soft',
].join(' ')

 * A group of items, divided from the one above it by the sheet's hairline.
 *
 * **The line is the group's own edge, not a decorative rule between two of them.** A sidebar in this
 * system is a stack of groups — the page's own destinations, then the collections under them — and
 * without an edge the last row of one group and the first row of the next sit exactly as close as
 * two rows inside either. The legend `Nav.Header` adds above it names the group; a group that is
 * named by an item instead (`Nav.Section` around an expandable parent) still gets the line.
 */

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-count`, pushed to the trailing edge so the numbers form a column down the side
 * rather than trailing each label at whatever length it happens to be — which is the whole reason a
 * sidebar carries counts at all.
 *
 * **It is quiet here; the sheet has it in the selected-yellow.** There the count appears in a horizontal
 * top bar, beside one or two other words. In a vertical sidebar two of them at `--warning` become the
 * loudest thing on the surface, while the labels they qualify — 70% white, 14px uppercase — read as the
 * quieter half of the pair. Yellow means *selection* everywhere else in this system, so spending it on
 * a number that is merely true costs it that meaning. The column stays: the alignment is what makes a
 * count scannable, not the colour.
 *
 * **In the rail it is a dot.** A 6px circle on the icon's shoulder says "there is something here" and
 * nothing more, which is all a 64px column can say; the number is still inside it, clipped, so the
 * screen reader that can read a count still gets one. It is not the accent, for the same reason the
 * wide panel's count is not the selected-yellow — the accent means *where you are*, and this dot would
 * be on a different row.
 */
const NAV_COUNT = [
  'ms-auto text-[11px] text-foreground/45 tabular-nums',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:absolute [[data-collapsed]_&]:top-1.5 [[data-collapsed]_&]:end-1.5',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:size-1.5 [[data-collapsed]_&]:overflow-hidden',
  '[[data-collapsed]_&]:rounded-full [[data-collapsed]_&]:bg-foreground/55',
].join(' ')

export interface NavProps<T extends object> extends Omit<
  AriaNavigationTreeProps<T>,
  'className'
> {
  ref?: React.Ref<HTMLDivElement>
  /**
   * The sidebar's surface and width. A function is passed through, since React Aria's own
   * `className` may be one.
   */
  className?: AriaNavigationTreeProps<T>['className']
  /**
   * The route you are on. Each item's `href` is matched against it, so this is the one prop that
   * makes a sidebar show where you are — and it is why the component has no `isCurrent` per item to
   * keep in sync.
   */
  selectedRoute?: AriaNavigationTreeProps<T>['selectedRoute']
  /**
   * The rail: the same tree at 64px, where an item is its icon. Labels stay in the markup and in the
   * accessibility tree at zero width, each one also becomes its item's tooltip, a count becomes the
   * dot on the icon's shoulder, and the disclosure waits in the row's corner until the row is
   * pointed at or focused. A tree and a rail are one component because they are one tree — the
   * alternative is two sidebars that drift apart.
   */
  isCollapsed?: boolean
  children?: React.ReactNode
}

/**
 * What a `Nav.Item` hands the `Nav.Label` inside it. Three things travel this way, and all three
 * are the item's rather than the label's: its destination, the string it is typed by, and the glyph
 * its row leads with.
 */
interface NavItemContextValue {
  href?: string
  textValue: string
  icon?: React.ReactNode
}

const NavItemContext = createContext<NavItemContextValue>({ textValue: '' })

/** Whether the enclosing `Nav` is a rail. One boolean for the whole subtree, read by every slot. */
const NavCollapsedContext = createContext(false)

export interface NavItemProps<T extends object = object> extends Omit<
  AriaNavigationTreeItemProps<T>,
  'className'
> {
  /**
   * The item's text, for keyboard type-ahead. Required rather than derived, and that is the honest
   * signature: an item's label here is markup — a count badge, often — and React Aria needs the
   * string it would actually be typed. It is also what the rail shows in place of a label.
   */
  textValue: string
  className?: AriaNavigationTreeItemProps<T>['className']
  /**
   * The glyph the row leads with, drawn in the column every row reserves whether or not it fills it.
   * A parent's icon is the same box as a child's, so a branch and the rows under it line up.
   *
   * It is a prop rather than a `Nav.Icon` slot inside the label. The label owns the row's edges —
   * the reserved box, the anchor, the trailing disclosure — and a slot would let the glyph land in
   * the middle of the link, or twice, and only the layout would know.
   */
  icon?: React.ReactNode
  /** A `Nav.Label`, and any nested `Nav.Item`s. */
  children: React.ReactNode
}

export interface NavLabelProps extends Omit<
  AriaNavigationTreeItemContentProps,
  'children'
> {
  /** What the item says. */
  children: React.ReactNode
  /** Overrides the enclosing `Nav.Item`'s `href`. Rarely wanted. */
  href?: string
}

export interface NavSectionProps<
  T extends object,
> extends AriaNavigationTreeSectionProps<T> {
  children?: React.ReactNode
}

export interface NavHeaderProps extends AriaNavigationTreeHeaderProps {
  children?: React.ReactNode
}

export interface NavCountProps extends React.HTMLAttributes<HTMLSpanElement> {
  children?: React.ReactNode
}

/** React Aria's `className` is either a string or a function of the item's state; join both. */
function joinClass(
  base: string,
  className: string | ((props: never) => string) | undefined,
  props: unknown,
): string {
  const extra =
    typeof className === 'function'
      ? (className as (p: unknown) => string)(props)
      : className
  return [base, extra].filter(Boolean).join(' ')
}

/**
 * One destination, or one that holds others. Use it as `Nav.Item`, inside a `Nav`. Nest a
 * `Nav.Item` inside it and it becomes the parent of a subtree — the nesting *is* the hierarchy, and
 * the indentation follows from it.
 *
 * Exported as `NavItem` only so tooling can resolve it; consume the compound form `Nav.Item`.
 */
export function NavItem<T extends object = object>({
  className,
  textValue,
  href,
  icon,
  children,
  ...props
}: NavItemProps<T>) {
  return (
    <NavItemContext.Provider value={{ href, textValue, icon }}>
      <AriaNavigationTreeItem
        href={href}
        textValue={textValue}
        className={(renderProps) =>
          joinClass(
            [
              NAV_ITEM,
              NAV_LEVEL[renderProps.level] ?? NAV_LEVEL[3],
              NAV_GUIDE[renderProps.level] ?? '',
            ]
              .filter(Boolean)
              .join(' '),
            className,
            renderProps,
          )
        }
        {...props}
      >
        {children}
      </AriaNavigationTreeItem>
    </NavItemContext.Provider>
  )
}

/**
 * What an item says. Use it as `Nav.Label`, as the first child of a `Nav.Item`.
 *
 * It draws the row: the icon's box, the link, the trailing disclosure. The icon comes from the
 * `Nav.Item` above it, because the *row* is where the column is reserved and the label is the thing
 * that fills it.
 *
 * Exported as `NavLabel` only so tooling can resolve it; consume the compound form `Nav.Label`.
 */
export function NavLabel({ children, href, ...props }: NavLabelProps) {
  const item = useContext(NavItemContext)
  const collapsed = useContext(NavCollapsedContext)
  const target = href ?? item.href

  const body = (
    <>
      <span aria-hidden="true" data-slot="icon" className={NAV_ICON}>
        {item.icon}
      </span>
      <span data-slot="text" className={NAV_TEXT}>
        {children}
      </span>
    </>
  )

  return (
    <AriaNavigationTreeItemContent {...props}>
      {({ hasChildItems, isExpanded }) => (
        <>
          {/* The state comes from the render props, not from a rule reaching down from the row —
              which is the arrangement the whole system avoids, because a group variant ties on
              specificity with its own child's rules and loses on source order. */}
          {target ? (
            collapsed ? (
              // **React Aria's `Link`, in the rail only, and only because of the tooltip.**
              // `TooltipTrigger` does not clone its child — it provides the trigger's props through
              // the Focusable context, which a bare `<a>` never reads, so the rail's tip would never
              // open. This renders the same `<a href>` the wide panel draws; the wide panel keeps the
              // plain one, since a tooltip it does not show is no reason to change the element the
              // rest of the library's links are not.
              <Tooltip delay={0}>
                <AriaLink href={target} className={NAV_LABEL_LINK}>
                  {body}
                </AriaLink>
                <Tooltip.Content>
                  <Tooltip.Text>{item.textValue}</Tooltip.Text>
                </Tooltip.Content>
              </Tooltip>
            ) : (
              // The anchor stays in the tab order, and that is not an oversight. The tree itself is
              // `tabindex="-1"` and its rows carry no tabindex at all — a *navigation* tree keeps a
              // virtual focus and expects its items to be real links, which are then the only things
              // here a keyboard can actually reach.
              <a href={target} className={NAV_LABEL_LINK}>
                {body}
              </a>
            )
          ) : (
            <span className={NAV_LABEL}>{body}</span>
          )}
          {hasChildItems ? (
            <AriaButton
              slot="chevron"
              className={`${NAV_CHEVRON} ${NAV_CHEVRON_RAIL}`}
            >
              <NavCaret expanded={isExpanded} />
            </AriaButton>
          ) : (
            // An empty box where the disclosure would be — see `NAV_END_GUTTER`: without it the
            // counts down the side lose their column, because a count rides the anchor's trailing
            // edge and a row with a chevron ends its anchor 24px sooner than one without.
            <span aria-hidden="true" className={NAV_END_GUTTER} />
          )}
        </>
      )}
    </AriaNavigationTreeItemContent>
  )
}

/** A chevron from two borders, pointing at the group when closed and down at it when open. */
/**
 * The disclosure chevron, exported because a tree and a nav point the same way — the row vocabulary
 * `NAV_ITEM` / `NAV_LEVEL` / `NAV_CHEVRON` is shared with `Tree`, and the glyph belongs with it.
 * `Nav` itself is the only consumer of the rest of this file.
 */
export function NavCaret({ expanded }: { expanded: boolean }) {
  return (
    <span
      aria-hidden="true"
      className={[
        'size-1.5 border-e border-b border-current',
        'motion-safe:transition-[rotate] motion-safe:duration-(--duration-fast) ease-pulse',
        expanded ? 'rotate-45' : 'rotate-[-45deg]',
      ].join(' ')}
    />
  )
}

/**
 * A group of items, divided from the one above it. Use it as `Nav.Section`.
 *
 * Exported as `NavSection` only so tooling can resolve it; consume the compound form `Nav.Section`.
 */
export function NavSection<T extends object>({
  className,
  children,
  ...props
}: NavSectionProps<T>) {
  return (
    <AriaNavigationTreeSection
      data-slot="section"
      className={[NAV_SECTION, className].filter(Boolean).join(' ')}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </AriaNavigationTreeSection>
  )
}

/**
 * A group's heading. Use it as `Nav.Header`.
 *
 * Exported as `NavHeader` only so tooling can resolve it; consume the compound form `Nav.Header`.
 */
export function NavHeader({ children, ...props }: NavHeaderProps) {
  return (
    <AriaNavigationTreeHeader className={NAV_HEADER} {...props}>
      <span data-slot="text" className={NAV_TEXT}>
        {children}
      </span>
    </AriaNavigationTreeHeader>
  )
}

/**
 * A count beside an item's label. Use it as `Nav.Count`.
 *
 * Exported as `NavCount` only so tooling can resolve it; consume the compound form `Nav.Count`.
 */
export function NavCount({ className, children, ...props }: NavCountProps) {
  return (
    <span
      data-slot="count"
      className={[NAV_COUNT, className].filter(Boolean).join(' ')}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </span>
  )
}

/**
 * Styled element. Not exported — `Nav` below is the public symbol, and docgen reads the JSDoc from
 * the *exported* declaration, not this one.
 */
function NavRoot<T extends object>({
  className,
  isCollapsed = false,
  children,
  ...props
}: NavProps<T>) {
  return (
    <NavCollapsedContext.Provider value={isCollapsed}>
      <AriaNavigationTree
        data-slot="nav"
        data-collapsed={isCollapsed || undefined}
        className={(renderProps) =>
          joinClass(
            `${NAV_PANEL} ${isCollapsed ? NAV_RAIL_WIDTH : NAV_WIDTH}`,
            className,
            renderProps,
          )
        }
        {...props}
      >
        {children}
      </AriaNavigationTree>
    </NavCollapsedContext.Provider>
  )
}

/**
 * A navigation sidebar — a nested, hierarchical set of links. **The sheet has no sidebar**: its two
 * navs, `dash-nav` and `page-nav`, are both horizontal top bars. The arrangement is therefore an
 * invention, but the behaviour is React Aria's `NavigationTree`, which is what a sidebar actually
 * is, and every visible part is the sheet's own vocabulary turned on its side.
 *
 * ```tsx
 * <Nav aria-label="Primary" selectedRoute="/monitors/fra1">
 *   <Nav.Item href="/" textValue="Overview" icon={<GridIcon />}>
 *     <Nav.Label>Overview</Nav.Label>
 *   </Nav.Item>
 *   <Nav.Item href="/monitors" textValue="Monitors" icon={<GaugeIcon />}>
 *     <Nav.Label>
 *       Monitors <Nav.Count>12</Nav.Count>
 *     </Nav.Label>
 *     <Nav.Item href="/monitors/fra1" textValue="fra1">
 *       <Nav.Label>fra1 · Frankfurt</Nav.Label>
 *     </Nav.Item>
 *   </Nav.Item>
 *   <Nav.Section>
 *     <Nav.Header>Account</Nav.Header>
 *     <Nav.Item href="/settings" textValue="Settings" icon={<GearIcon />}>
 *       <Nav.Label>Settings</Nav.Label>
 *     </Nav.Item>
 *   </Nav.Section>
 * </Nav>
 * ```
 *
 * ### `selectedRoute` is the whole of "where am I"
 *
 * There is no `isCurrent` to set per item and keep in sync with the router. One string is matched
 * against every `href`, and the tree marks not only the item that matches but its **ancestors** —
 * `data-current-ancestor` — which is the thing a top bar never needed and a tree cannot do without.
 * The current row is washed and its label takes the accent; an ancestor comes up to full strength
 * and goes no further, because two accented labels would stop saying which one you are on.
 *
 * ### The nesting is the hierarchy
 *
 * A `Nav.Item` inside a `Nav.Item` is its child. The indentation follows from the depth React Aria
 * reports, not from anything the consumer writes — so moving an item one level is moving a line of
 * JSX, and nothing else has to be kept in step.
 *
 * ### The label contains a count, so the text is passed separately
 *
 * `textValue` is required, and that is the honest signature rather than an annoyance: the label is
 * markup, often with a badge in it, and keyboard type-ahead needs the string someone would actually
 * type. Deriving it from the rendered label would pick up the count. In the rail it is also the one
 * thing about an item that survives: it is the tooltip and the accessible name.
 *
 * ### A navigation tree is links, not buttons
 *
 * `aria-label` matters more here than on a single-purpose page: a screen reader lists every nav on
 * the page by its label, and "Primary" is what tells them which one this is.
 *
 * ### `isCollapsed` is a rail, not a hidden sidebar
 *
 * The same tree at 64px. Labels keep their place in the accessibility tree, a count becomes the dot
 * on the icon's shoulder, each item's `textValue` becomes its tooltip, and the disclosure waits in
 * the row's corner until the row is pointed at or focused. What the rail does *not* do is take
 * anything away: every item is still a link, every branch still opens, and the way back is the state
 * the consumer already holds — `isCollapsed` is a prop, not internal state, because the control that
 * toggles it belongs beside the sidebar rather than inside it.
 */
export const Nav = Object.assign(NavRoot, {
  Item: NavItem,
  Label: NavLabel,
  Section: NavSection,
  Header: NavHeader,
  Count: NavCount,
})

  AriaOverlayArrowProps,
  'className'

export function OverlayArrow({ className, ...props }: OverlayArrowProps) {

    <AriaOverlayArrow
      data-slot="overlay-arrow"
      className={OVERLAY_ARROW_POSITION}
      {...props}

export interface ToggleButtonProps extends Omit<

  | 'children'

  | 'defaultSelected'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'isDisabled'
  | 'isPending'
  | 'onPress'

  onPress?: AriaToggleButtonProps['onPress']

  variant?: NonNullable<ButtonProps['variant']>

 * <ToggleButton isSelected={live} onChange={setLive}>Live</ToggleButton>

 * and `popover.ts` make, except that here the shared thing was already in one file and only needed

  color = 'primary',
  size = 'md',
  className,
  children,
  ...props
